I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over fifty years. My sons went to work in the city years ago, so now it's mostly me, sometimes with my wife helping with lighter work. I can't manage as much land as I used to — my back gives me trouble — so I keep it to 8 mu. I hire machines for the heavy jobs: plowing, planting, harvesting. I pay for that out of what I sell.

In Quzhou, everybody grows wheat in the winter and corn in the summer on the same fields. That's just how it is here. The soil knows these crops. The water table is reachable by the village tube wells. The grain station buys whatever I grow. I'm not going to try vegetables or cotton or anything unfamiliar at my age. Too much risk, too much extra work I can't do.

For wheat, I'll use the improved variety seeds — the county agricultural office distributed them again this year and they yielded well last season. I'll put down compound fertilizer before planting and spread urea when the wheat greens up in spring. I irrigate four times: once before winter sets in, once in early spring, once at jointing, once at heading. I spray for aphids and rust in spring — two passes is usually enough.

After wheat harvest in June, I plant hybrid corn immediately on the same fields — no-till, straight into the stubble. The machine does it fast. Corn gets more nitrogen than wheat, split — some at planting, more when it's knee-high. Rain is usually enough for corn here in summer, but I'll irrigate once if July is dry like last year.

I keep records in my head the same way my father did. I don't change much year to year because what works, works.
